name: Read the signal: which dimension is weak?
note: Each is a moment from an AI-assisted round where the final code is fine. Name the rubric dimension the behaviour actually exposes — that's what the interviewer is scoring.

items.prompt: A candidate ships the AI's solution fast and correct. Asked 'what happens on an empty list?', they re-read the code for thirty seconds before answering.
candidates: Comprehension (Technical Correctness) — they accepted code they hadn't internalized; the re-reading is the tell that they're reasoning about it for the first time, live
Communication — they just need to answer more confidently next time
Trade-off Awareness — they should have picked a different algorithm
Nothing is weak — correct code that passes the tests is a full pass
items.correct: Comprehension (Technical Correctness) — they accepted code they hadn't internalized; the re-reading is the tell that they're reasoning about it for the first time, live
items.explanation: Comprehension is the ability to reason about code you didn't type. The fix is the review stage: read the diff and trace the boundaries before you say 'done', so the empty-list answer is instant instead of excavated. Re-reading to answer is reviewing too late, in front of the interviewer.
items.principle: If you have to re-read it to answer, you reviewed it too late.

items.prompt: Given an ambiguous spec, a candidate immediately prompts for a full implementation and builds something polished — that solves a slightly different problem than intended.
candidates: Strategic clarification (Trade-off Awareness) — they delegated before pinning the problem; one clarifying question, or a restated assumption, would have aimed the whole effort correctly
Comprehension — they didn't understand the code the AI produced
Evaluation Rigor — they simply didn't write enough test cases
Communication — they only needed to type and talk faster
items.correct: Strategic clarification (Trade-off Awareness) — they delegated before pinning the problem; one clarifying question, or a restated assumption, would have aimed the whole effort correctly
items.explanation: The most expensive AI-assisted mistake is a confident solution to the wrong problem — automation makes producing it fast and polished. Clarifying is the loop's first stage and cheap insurance; interviewers specifically watch whether you confirm the target before you delegate.
items.principle: Polished output aimed at the wrong target is the costliest thing AI makes easy.

items.prompt: The candidate's code passes the tests they were handed. They declare it done with no cases of their own — then it fails on a boundary the interviewer probes.
candidates: Verification (Evaluation Rigor) — passing handed-down tests isn't verifying; they never defined what 'right' means beyond the given cases, so the boundary was never a gate
Comprehension — they understood it fine, so nothing here is wrong
Communication — they explained it clearly, so it should count as a pass
Trade-off Awareness — they merely chose the wrong data structure
items.correct: Verification (Evaluation Rigor) — passing handed-down tests isn't verifying; they never defined what 'right' means beyond the given cases, so the boundary was never a gate
items.explanation: Verification is deciding the standard and checking against it (prompt → review → run → confirm). The fix is preregistering invariants and tests before prompting, so boundaries are gates the solution must satisfy, not surprises the interviewer finds for you.
items.principle: Given tests check what someone already feared; verification checks what you decided matters.
